Nothing could be more appropriate

been a stalwart among the three current
West Coast chapters (the Zeta Zeta at the
University of British Columbia and the
Epsilon at the University of California at
Berkeley being the other two active
chapters). The Theta Theta Chapter has
built a well-deserved reputation among

in every aspect of life on the University
of Washington campus. Many of us on

occurrences of the early 1970's when the
Theta Theta at one time was reduced to
just six undergraduates. Nothing, how
ever, could deter the spirit of the Theta
Theta's alumni, who carefully assisted the
chapter to rebuild its numbers and
strength back to its current resurgence.
The Executive Council held one of its
meetings in Seattle in February, 1976,
as a part of that rejuvenation effort. To
day, we are all proud to join the brothers
of the Theta Theta in celebrating the 70th
anniversary of what is again one of our
preeminent chapters!

RHO REVIVAL
(Madison, WI) Last October the Exec
utive Council placed the Rho Chapter on
"Review" status in light of its long
standing operational problems. The
Chapter's undergraduate and alumni of
ficers were advised of this action and asked
to achieve certain minimum standards
pirior to the Executive Council's June
meeting, at which time a
thorough eval
uation would be made and a decision
reached on the future status of the Rho.
At the Executive Council's June meet
ing, at which four alumni members of the
Rho were represented (unfortunately no
undergraduates were able to attend),
comprehensive reports from the Rho un
dergraduates and alumni and from staff
members who had visited the Chapter
were reviewed with great care. After a
long, detaded, and painful discussion, the
Executive Council decided (subject to re
view by the 143rd Convention) that suf
ficient progress had not been made and
that the Rho Chapter should be declared
inactive. The Council further affirmed its
commitment to reactivation at the ear
liest feasible time.
The Rho Chapter was well represented
at the Convention by both alumni and
undergraduates, who petitioned the
Convention for a reversal of the Execu
tive Council's action. In recognition of
the Rho members' earnest appreciation
of their situation and their dedication to
ward achieving a set of very concrete goals
during the coming year, the 143rd Con
vention granted the Rho Chapter full rec
ognition. This decision, it was agreed by
all parties, will be subject to final review
by the Executive Council in the spring
of 1987, at which time the Chapter's
progress in attainment of these pre-determined goals will be evaluated. The
Fraternity staff will be working closely
and diligently with the Rho over the com
ing months to assist them in every way
possible in accomplishing this objective.

(Durham, NC) Heartiest congratulations

Delta '88. We commend the Chi Delta
Chapter for its commitment to academic
excellence and wish them continued suc
cess!

(Bethlehem, PA) The telephone rang
while Brothers Robie, Kerstein, and Poor
were attending an interfraternity meet
ing on insurance in Indianapolis. Word
came that the Eta Chapter house had just
suffered a fire! How ironic! Fortunately,
most fortunately, there were no injuries,
and the damage was limited to $4,000-
$5,000, fully covered by insurance. It
could have been a whole lot worse.
Stately Eta Chapter house at Lehigh
University escapes significant fire dam
age thanks to effective heat and fire de
tection equipment.
When the Chapter meeting ended
around 11:00 p.m. on September 17, the
candles were extinguished and the lights
turned off. Perhaps the closing of the
Chapter Room door dislodged one of the
candles, and the still-hot embers may have
ignited some flammable cloth. About 2:00
a.m. the heat detector was activated; the
alarm rang throughout the house and in
Lehigh's security headquarters. Fire
fighters arrived minutes later, and the
blaze was extinguished promptly, leaving
a
damaged area in one corner of the room
and soot covering the furniture and walls.

Sigma Chapter
Brown University
It is hard to believe that the Sigma was reactivated only last
spring when one looks at a list of its accomplishments. From
a core group of 17, their numbers have grown to 42. They have
participated in numerous campus and community activities,
most notably by assisting a drug rehabilitation center in raising
$14,000. They were granted University housing last fall in
recognition of their superb efforts and have been praised by
the administration, including a letter from the President. Most
impressive of all, the Association of Fraternity Presidents at
Brown awarded them the "Fraternity of the Year" award. Their
motivation and dedication toward restoring the Sigma Chapter
to its distinguished place within Psi Upsilon and the Brown
community make them deserving recipients of this award.
Chi Chapter
Cornell University
The Chi Chapter has been located off campus since its reac
tivation in January, 1985, waiting to reoccupy its chapter house
until its numbers had grown and its operation solidified (the
Chi happily was permitted to reoccupy Two Forest Park Lane
this fall). While living in the off-campus facility, the members
of the Chi performed a valuable public service by taking a
leadership role in Collegetown Neighborhood Council. The
Assistant Dean for Off-Campus Life writes: "The wdlingness
to go out of their way to work on Council projects and the
dedication that they exemplified is one of the most admirable
acts in the history of the Councd. ... It has been an honor to
be associated with these fine young men. ... Psi Upsdon has
proven they are truly leaders in their community." The initi
ative and selfless energy of the members of the Chi Chapter
in this worthwhile endeavor to improve their neighborhood
were rewarded with an Award of Distinction.
Omicron Chapter
University of Illinois
The Omicron has long been a leader in philanthropic activ
ities. In the recent past it has raised significant funds for Project
Concern through its Walk for Mankind. Last year the Omicron
undertook a new project �
the sponsorship of downstate Il
linois' only TRI-FED sanctioned triathlon (running, swimming,
and bicycling), the proceeds of which were directed toward the
restoration of the Statue of Liberty. Thirty dedicated brothers
spent a year preparing for the event, which attracted 600 par
ticipants, and almost everyone in the house made some kind
of contribution toward its success. The Omicron has earned
campus and community recognition for their efforts, and Psi
Upsilon is proud to honor them with an Award of Distinction.
Epsilon Nu Chapter
Michigan State University
Several years ago the Epsilon Nu adopted as its philanthropy
the Beekman Center for the Mentally Retarded, a local East
Lansing home for children. Throughout the year the Chapter
hosts a variety of events for the residents of the Home. For
instance, the brothers help the kids celebrate both Christmas
and Easter each year with a fun-filled party, replete with good
ies, gifts, and guests (Santa or the Bunny). To quote a member
of the Epsilon Nu, ". . . it has become a labor of love for all
of the brothers ... an invaluable experience ... it benefits
both the kids and ourselves ... it allows us to reach out. ..."
Psi Upsilon applauds the Epsilon Nu for this worthwhile com
munity service project and deems them deserving recipients
of an Award of Distinction.

Brother Harriman went on to serve as

President Kennedy referred to him as

ers," says TIME magazine, "the way other
men collect stamps."
Brother Harriman was born in 1891,

Harriman. He was raised in the family's
American approximation of a barony �

the Ramapo Valley on the west side of

West Point, New York. A winding S'/z
mile road or a funicular railway brought

imposing stables, a polo field, a track for

supplied West Point with milk since be
fore the Spanish-American War.
As part of what he describes as the

Harriman was remembered as a modest,

CONVENTION '86
while most of the nation was
suffering
through the dog days of August, more than one
hundred Psi Upsilon undergraduates and alum
ni were rolling up their sleeves and tackling the
business of the Fraternity. The event was, of
course, the 143rd Convention, held under the
auspices of the Theta Theta Chapter at the Uni
versity of Washington.
Delegates spent August 20 through August
24 attending legislative meetings, workshops,
seminars, and committee meetings, all ofwhich
helped give them a better knowledge of how
Psi U operiates. Business meetings were inter
spersed with some dynamic presentations and
highly effective speakers, including William P.
Gerberding, President of the University of
Washington; Dr. Robert H. Shaffer, Dean
Emeritus at Indiana University; Brewster
Denny, Professor of Public Affairs at UW and
a member of the "founding family" of Seattle;
John B. Fery, Theta Theta '52, Chairman of the
Board and Chief Executive Officer of Boise Cas
cade; and James A. Swanke, Jr., Rho '80, na
tionally recognized expert in the field of risk
management, which was the major focus of this
Convention.
Official business was not the only item on the
agenda, though, and delegates found oppor
tunities to enjoy Seattle's hospitality and the
best weather of the summer. Some arrived early
or stayed late in order to include an excursion
to the International Expo just two hours away
in Vancouver, British Columbia. Others found
time to visit the natural wonders of both Mount
Rainier and Olympic National Park. Hopefully
everyone explored the major attractions in Se
attle, where shoppers, sightseers, and sports
men could find a multitude of diversions in this
magnificent city rising from the Puget Sound.

The Convention itself afforded an
opportu
nity to partake of Seattle's breathtaking beauty
during the Emerald City Cruise. Brothers and
guests boarded the "Spirit of '76" for a threehour trip through the Puget Sound and the
adjoining lakes, Washington and Union. The
fraternal experience was heightened by a set
ting which was truly spectacular.
Most memorable of all, perhaps, were the
brothers met, friends made, and stories ex
changed (some true!). The annual Convention
is one of the few times when it is possible to
gauge the true scope of Psi Upsilon. With most
Chapters represented, there was the oppor
tunity to see the Fraternity as a whole, span
ning the continent and her finest academic in
stitutions. Brothers from every part of North
America, from the class of 1923 to the class of
1990, were joined by a common bond.
It would be impossible to discuss the 143rd
Convention without recognizing some impor
tant contributors to its success. At the top of
this list are Richard Cuff '87, undergraduate
president of the Theta Theta; Bill Borkowski,
Theta Theta '88; and Glen Hubbard, Theta
Theta '88. Strong assists go to the entire un
dergraduate membership of the Theta Theta,
who worked tirelessly to make this Convention
the success that it was.
Delegates departed the Pacific Northwest
weary but fulfilled. While in Seattle, they dis
cussed, debated, argued, learned, shared, and
grew. They left with a renewed enthusiasm for
Psi Upsilon and a heightened anticipation of
the 144th Convention in New York City!

It is with great pleasure and pride that we present this report of
the success of the 1985-86 Annual Giving program. A new high of

average gift of $65.58, certainly one of the highest averages in the
fraternity world.
Once again the alumni of Psi Upsilon have set new records in
giving, thereby enabling us to extend the warm hand of brotherhood
to yet another generation of fine undergraduates. This enthusiastic
response is truly heartwarming, and the Executive Council extends
its heartiest and most sincere thanks for each measure of assistance,
large and small.
The following record of statistics and lists, which represents gifts
received from July 1, 1985 through June 30, 1986 (gifts received
subsequent to June 30 have been credited to the 1986-87 program),
serves to honor the faithful and supportive members of Psi Upsilon
who, by their generosity, have enabled the Fraternity to move
forward on its distinguished course.
This year we have initiated a new concept of recognizing the suin
total of contributions which an alumnus has made to the Annual
Giving program since its inception in 1964. New levels of support
have been named, borrowing from some of our great Psi U songs, to
acknowledge each alumnus' cumulative giving record to the
Fraternity. Names in bolder print represent leadership contributors
(1985-86 gift of $50 or more), and years of consecutive giving are
shown in parentheses after the name and class of donors.
As we chart the course for the future, we must ask our alumni to
raise their sights still further, so that we can maintain and even
expand the scope of Psi Upsilon's services and activities in behalf of
our undergraduate Chapters. The 1986-87 budget calls for $156,800
in Annual Giving contributions. Of great encouragement is the fact
that this year's program is off to a resounding start. We beUeve that
the alumni of Psi Upsilon again will rise to the challenge of meeting,
perhaps even exceeding, this ambitious goal!
